{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01S4jzBDcS5nqda8hKjVMQhW","type":"tool_result","content":"total 0\ndrwxr-xr-x@ 3 <user>  staff   96 Aug  3 07:37 .\ndrwxr-xr-x@ 6 <user>  staff  192 Aug 25 17:34 ..\n-rw-r--r--@ 1 <user>  staff    0 Aug  3 07:37 .gitkeep\n---\n# nurb design doctrine\n\nPrinted via `nurb rules`. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\nthat says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **A counterbore prints mouth toward the bed, and that floats its ceiling.** The shelf the screw head bears on is laid flat over the open pocket, and the smaller hole's first rim is a circle drawn on air; the `hole_ceiling` finding is this exact case, and it appears on any hole rising out of a bridged roof, not just screw pockets. Never answer it with supports inside a pocket nobody can clean: cut the hole with `counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth)`, which steps the transition through two sacrificial bridge layers, a slot bridged chord-to-chord across the pocket and the same slot turned ninety degrees across the first, so each layer spans only what the one before it laid and the whole stack prints support-free. Reach for it whenever a design wants a screw head, a nut, or any wider recess on the bed side of a hole.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **A large first layer peels its corners as it cools.** Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part, and the pull lands hardest on a sharp plan corner, farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. Past about 20,000mm2 of first layer the accumulated pull beats corner adhesion, and `warp_risk` names the corners that will lift. The fixes are in the outline, which is what makes this a CAD problem where elephant's foot is not: round the vertical corners at 8mm or more, so the peel front is a curve instead of a point, and give a big plate a ribbed floor rather than a solid slab, which is stiffer per gram and halves what contracts. A 1mm polish chamfer is not relief here; it moves the point half a millimetre. The brim and the clean bed are the slicer's share, and they treat the symptom the outline caused. Material multiplies the pull: the threshold is calibrated on PLA, and naming what the machine prints in `printer.toml`, `material = \"abs\"` next to the profile line, tightens it fivefold, because ABS contracts 1 to 2% as it cools where PLA holds under half a percent. PETG judges as PLA, ASA as ABS, and PC and PP tighter still. At the far end the rule stops being about corners: a bed-covering part in ABS, ASA or PC is the wrong material, and the fix is PETG or PLA, not a wider brim.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n- **A pin under 5mm across is perimeters with nothing inside.** There is no room between the walls for infill, so a thin printed pin is a tube, loaded in bending at the weakest weld it has, its base. Under 3mm the nozzle is re-melting each ring as it lays the next, and the pin may not survive its own printing. `pin` fires on a free-standing vertical cylinder taller than twice its diameter; a stub or a locating nub has nothing to lever with and stays silent. The fixes, in order: thicken it past 5mm, give its base a structural chamfer sized like any other loaded junction, or model the hole instead and press in a metal pin, the same trade the fastener rules already make, because off-the-shelf steel beats printed plastic everywhere they compete.\n\n### Holes\n\n- **No hole under 2mm across.** Below that the perimeters converge and the bore prints as a smear or closes outright. A locating hole that small is a drill's job: model a 1mm dimple to centre the bit and let steel cut the diameter.\n- **Every vertical bore prints small**, by the same few tenths the fastener table's medium column already absorbs for screws, and the physics does not care that a dowel or a shaft is not a screw. Any bore gets the medium column's slack against its rod's true diameter, and when the diameter genuinely matters, printing is the wrong finisher: model half a millimetre under and drill to size, because a drill holds a tolerance no printer does.\n- **A horizontal hole's crown is a bridge.** Under the printer's span limit no rule minds it, but the crown sags into the bore and prints out of round exactly where a fit would bear. Prefer standing the hole vertical; the orientation rules usually allow it. When the axis cannot move and roundness matters, roof the bore with two 45 degree chords meeting in a point above the crown, a teardrop, which is the counterbore's idea turned sideways: every layer leans on the one before instead of spanning air.\n\n### Fasteners\n\n**A published standard is not a guess.** Measurements says never improvise a dimension, and a screw is the one place that rule gets misread: nobody has to measure an M3 cap screw, because ISO fixed its head at 5.5mm across in every box you will ever open. Take these from the table and spend the question you saved on something the table cannot answer.\n\n| Thread | Clearance hole, close | medium | Cap head dia | Cap head height | Nut across flats | across corners | Nut thickness |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| M2 | 2.2 | 2.4 | 3.8 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 4.4 | 1.6 |\n| M2.5 | 2.7 | 2.9 | 4.5 | 2.5 | 5.0 | 5.5 | 2.0 |\n| M3 | 3.2 | 3.4 | 5.5 | 3.0 | 5.5 | 6.1 | 2.4 |\n| M4 | 4.3 | 4.5 | 7.0 | 4.0 | 7.0 | 7.7 | 3.2 |\n| M5 | 5.3 | 5.5 | 8.5 | 5.0 | 8.0 | 8.8 | 4.7 |\n| M6 | 6.4 | 6.6 | 10.0 | 6.0 | 10.0 | 11.1 | 5.2 |\n| M8 | 8.4 | 9.0 | 13.0 | 8.0 | 13.0 | 14.4 | 6.8 |\n\nClearance is ISO 273, cap head is ISO 4762 socket head, nut is ISO 4032 hex. In mm. Across corners is the one a round pocket has to clear, and it is the number people reach for the wrong column of: an M3 nut is 5.5 across the flats and will not go into a 5.5 hole.\n\n**Reach for the medium column.** A printed hole comes out under its modelled size, by a few tenths that vary with the machine, the material and how fast the perimeter was laid, so the close column is a fit you have to earn with a coupon rather than one you can assume. Medium already carries that much slack, which is why it is the default here and close is the exception a fit coupon has justified.\n\n**Give a screw head its pocket through `counterbore`, never a plain wider hole.** Head diameter plus about 0.4, head height plus a layer, and the pocket faces the bed with the shaft rising out of it: that is the shape the table above is sized for, and it is the shape `counterbore` cuts.\n\n**A nut pocket is a hex prism, and `counterbore` cannot cut one.** It cuts a cylinder, so the pocket is modelled by hand: `extrude(RegularPolygon(across_corners / 2, 6), thickness + 0.2)` sized on the across-corners column, or a round pocket at across-corners plus 0.2 if the nut is free to spin. A hex takes about 0.2 of slack across the flats, and rotating the prism so a flat rather than a point faces up prints a cleaner socket. It floats its own ceiling exactly the way a screw head does and earns the same `hole_ceiling` finding, so the two sacrificial bridge layers still apply; that trick is the part of `counterbore` worth copying, and the cylinder is not.\n\n**Heat-set inserts are the exception that proves the rule.** Their boss diameter is set by the insert a particular vendor ships and not by any standard, the same nominal thread differs by half a millimetre between brands, and the number that matters is the one on the bag in the user's drawer. Ask, or measure one, and record it with `measured()`.\n\n**Never model a thread under M5.** A printed thread below that is slivers arranged in a helix: the crests print as smears, and what does print strips the first time it is torqued. The hardware above is the answer, a nut in its pocket or a heat-set insert, and even past M5 a modelled thread is a choice the card justifies, never a default.\n\n**A loaded hole earns a fastener diameter of wall.** An M5 screw wants 5mm of material around its bore. Thinner, and the boss bulges as the screw seats, then splits along a layer weld, which is the one direction a boss cannot spare. The clearance columns say where the hole is; this says how much part has to be around it.\n\n### Fits between printed parts\n\nThe fastener table covers steel meeting plastic. Two printed faces that work together get a designed gap of their own, sized by what the pair does, and stated as the total extra on the opening: a bore over its shaft, a pocket over its tongue, whatever dimension the pair shares.\n\n| Fit | Extra on the opening | What it feels like |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| press | 0.1 | driven together once, holds by friction |\n| snug | 0.2 | slides on by hand, no rattle |\n| moving | 0.3 | swings and slides through its whole travel, the hinge floor |\n| free | 0.5 | drops in every time, on any printer, in any material |\n\nIn mm. The table is where a fit starts, never what lets it skip the coupon: anything fit-critical is still measured, printed as a coupon, and corrected before the part prints. Two limits: below 0.1 is not a tighter press, it is a bind that varies by machine, and a moving pair never ships at less than 0.3, because the 0.2 that swings freely on the printer that made it seizes on the next one.\n\n## Print orientation\n\nParts print the way they are modelled, +z up, and for most parts that is the end of it. Orientation becomes a decision in exactly two situations: an overhang a corbel cannot carry without disfiguring the part, and a load that wraps a corner, where no flat orientation keeps every member strong.\n\n- **The two remedies for an overhang finding are a corbel and a tilt.** Reach for the corbel first: it is local, it keeps the part on its natural face, and it disappears into the design. Reach for the tilt when the whole part fights the bed. An open box printed upright wants support inside; printed flat it has one huge first layer that warps and three finishes that do not match; stood on a corner at 45 degrees, nothing needs support and every face is printed as perimeters, one finish.\n- **Layer bonds are about half strength**, measured near 50% of in-plane tensile for PLA and worse for ASA. A part loaded around a corner, which is every bracket and every L, has no flat orientation that keeps both legs loading in-plane: one of them always pulls its layers apart. Stood at 45 degrees neither does, and the load path never lies in a single weld plane. A tilt moves the weak plane rather than deleting it, so it is not automatic: a hook printed at an angle fails at the same load with the break somewhere else. It earns its keep on corners, not on straight pulls.\n- **`stand(part, tilt, axis, facet)` is the verb.** It rotates the part about a horizontal axis, seats it, and shaves the down corner flat, because a part standing on an unshaved corner meets the bed along a single extrusion line, and that line peels. The facet is 2mm minimum, measured across the flat. 45 degrees is the usual tilt and is not sacred: a shallow part stands at whatever angle brings everything inside the limit. Run the polish pass before standing, in the functional orientation.\n- **Stand a part on the corner that grounds every region, and prefer the lowest stance that does.** For an L that is the outside of its elbow, legs up in a V. The sign of the roll depends on which way the model faces, so check rather than reason: the same L rolled the other way stands on the end of one leg as a chevron, still grounded, still legal, but 60% taller on the same facet, and height on a facet is what spends the adhesion margin. The stance to refuse is the tent, elbow up, one leg's tip hanging in air, and it is easy to miss by eye because nothing about it looks steep: every face of the floating tip can sit at exactly 45 degrees, silent to the overhang rule. The `floating` rule fails any region whose first layer has nothing to sit on and `stability` judges the height, so `nurb check` on the stood variant settles the corner choice. Past grounded, inside the limit, and low, the tilt is taste: what remains is where the facet scar lands, which is the user's call.\n- **A diagonal print is a variant, and it is offered, never imposed.** The facet is cut from visible geometry, and whether that corner may go is not a printability question: only the user knows whether it shows. The pattern is a bool parameter, `diagonal=False`, that applies `stand()` when true, and a card variant that sets it, so it builds, checks against its own baselines, exports its own STL and shows in the viewer like any variant. Give the variant a `note` saying what the tilt buys and costs in plain words, \"prints tilted on a flattened corner: no supports, and stronger across the corner\", never in the doctrine's. Build it speculatively and link it, `?part=x&variant=x_diagonal`; the user judges by looking, and two lines delete it if they pass.\n- **Past about twenty times the facet width in height, adhesion is holding a lever, and `stand()` grows fins.** A compact part holds its facet by first-layer adhesion; a tall one needs support fins modelled into the part, never slicer supports, whose loose grip lets warp tension spring the part free mid-print. The recipe is print-farm practice with fixed numbers, so it is generated rather than judged: a thin blade at each side of the part hugging the lean across a small gap, each on a 1mm pad for its own adhesion, joined to the part only by horizontal tines a single layer tall and a bead wide, about 0.5 x 0.5mm, five or so, biased toward the bottom where the young print is least stable. This file is the single source; harness files point at it\nrather than repeating it.\n\nThese are standing rules for FDM-printed parts, and several are vetoes rather than\npreferences. Most of them are physics, so they outlive any particular CAD kernel. The\nones that are specific to OCCT are marked as such and were measured, not reasoned.\n\n## The part contract\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import *\n\n@part\ndef dispenser(width=80.0, height=120.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, height, wall)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n```\n\nKeyword defaults are the parameters. That one declaration feeds the agent, the CLI, the\nviewer, the tests, and any future configurator. Never add a parallel `PARAMS` dict; the\ntwo would drift.\n\n**Write a continuous dimension as a float.** The type of a default is the only thing\nthat says whether a value is a count or a measurement, and the viewer reads it: an `int`\ndefault gets a slider that steps by one, a `float` default one that moves continuously.\n`bracket_count=4` is a count and `chamfer_size=1.0` is a millimetre, so the trailing\n`.0` is doing work. Nothing else has to be declared, and there is no annotation to keep\nin sync, because the type is already there in the signature.\n\n`draft` is optional and injected by the runtime, never passed by a caller. When it is\ntrue, skip the polish pass. It is worth about 20% on a real part, not the 18x a cube\nsuggests.\n\nReturn one solid. A function that returns two loose bodies still reports a plausible\nbounding box and still exports, so nothing downstream catches it.\n\n**When a configuration cannot work, refuse it with `reject`, never a bare raise.** A holder whose hole is narrower than the tool it holds should not build, and `reject(\"drill_hole_width 14 is under the 14.27mm pin vise plus print shrink: raise it above 14.77\", param=\"drill_hole_width\")` is how a part says so. The message states what is wrong and what value fixes it; `param` names the offending parameter so the viewer marks its slider. The viewer presents a refusal as a limit of the design, in amber with the last good geometry still on screen, where a bare `ValueError` arrives as a red traceback that reads as the part being broken. Guard only what would print wrong or not work at all; taste stays a slider.\n\n## Printability\n\n- **Minimum wall 2 to 3mm**, except where fit geometry says otherwise. Fit-critical\n  dimensions are already tuned; do not round them for tidiness.\n- **Print support-free. No floating features.** Parts print bottom down, building up in\n  +z, so every functional feature is grounded. A vertical extrusion or a vertical\n  through hole is self-supporting. A shelf, loop, or band floated partway up with a gap\n  underneath is not.\n- **A counterbore prints mouth toward the bed, and that floats its ceiling.** The shelf the screw head bears on is laid flat over the open pocket, and the smaller hole's first rim is a circle drawn on air; the `hole_ceiling` finding is this exact case, and it appears on any hole rising out of a bridged roof, not just screw pockets. Never answer it with supports inside a pocket nobody can clean: cut the hole with `counterbore(hole_dia, head_dia, head_depth, depth)`, which steps the transition through two sacrificial bridge layers, a slot bridged chord-to-chord across the pocket and the same slot turned ninety degrees across the first, so each layer spans only what the one before it laid and the whole stack prints support-free. Reach for it whenever a design wants a screw head, a nut, or any wider recess on the bed side of a hole.\n- **Corbel rule.** Grounded does not mean a column to the bed. Support-free means no\n  layer overhanging past 45 degrees. Where material would run to the plate only to\n  satisfy printing, carry the feature on a 45 degree underside instead: a short vertical\n  tip of 4 to 6mm below the floor at the front face, then a 45 degree plane falling back\n  into the body. Every layer then overhangs by at most half a bead and bonds to the wall\n  behind it.\n- **Corbels are always exactly 45 degrees**, the same as every other facet. Never\n  steepen one or match it to a ratio. Let the landing point fall where 45 degrees puts\n  it. Mismatched facet angles are a veto: every facet on the part, cosmetic or\n  structural or corbel, has to read as one system.\n- **A large first layer peels its corners as it cools.** Every layer shrinks as it cools and pulls toward the middle of the part, and the pull lands hardest on a sharp plan corner, farthest from the middle and holding on at a point. Past about 20,000mm2 of first layer the accumulated pull beats corner adhesion, and `warp_risk` names the corners that will lift. The fixes are in the outline, which is what makes this a CAD problem where elephant's foot is not: round the vertical corners at 8mm or more, so the peel front is a curve instead of a point, and give a big plate a ribbed floor rather than a solid slab, which is stiffer per gram and halves what contracts. A 1mm polish chamfer is not relief here; it moves the point half a millimetre. The brim and the clean bed are the slicer's share, and they treat the symptom the outline caused. Material multiplies the pull: the threshold is calibrated on PLA, and naming what the machine prints in `printer.toml`, `material = \"abs\"` next to the profile line, tightens it fivefold, because ABS contracts 1 to 2% as it cools where PLA holds under half a percent. PETG judges as PLA, ASA as ABS, and PC and PP tighter still. At the far end the rule stops being about corners: a bed-covering part in ABS, ASA or PC is the wrong material, and the fix is PETG or PLA, not a wider brim.\n- **Elephant's foot is a slicer setting**, not a CAD problem. Do not model around it.\n- **A pin under 5mm across is perimeters with nothing inside.** There is no room between the walls for infill, so a thin printed pin is a tube, loaded in bending at the weakest weld it has, its base. Under 3mm the nozzle is re-melting each ring as it lays the next, and the pin may not survive its own printing. `pin` fires on a free-standing vertical cylinder taller than twice its diameter; a stub or a locating nub has nothing to lever with and stays silent. The fixes, in order: thicken it past 5mm, give its base a structural chamfer sized like any other loaded junction, or model the hole instead and press in a metal pin, the same trade the fastener rules already make, because off-the-shelf steel beats printed plastic everywhere they compete.\n\n### Holes\n\n- **No hole under 2mm across.** Below that the perimeters converge and the bore prints as a smear or closes outright. A locating hole that small is a drill's job: model a 1mm dimple to centre the bit and let steel cut the diameter.\n- **Every vertical bore prints small**, by the same few tenths the fastener table's medium column already absorbs for screws, and the physics does not care that a dowel or a shaft is not a screw. When the axis cannot move and roundness matters, roof the bore with two 45 degree chords meeting in a point above the crown, a teardrop, which is the counterbore's idea turned sideways: every layer leans on the one before instead of spanning air.\n\n### Fasteners\n\n**A published standard is not a guess.** Measurements says never improvise a dimension, and a screw is the one place that rule gets misread: nobody has to measure an M3 cap screw, because ISO fixed its head at 5.5mm across in every box you will ever open. In mm. Across corners is the one a round pocket has to clear, and it is the number people reach for the wrong column of: an M3 nut is 5.5 across the flats and will not go into a 5.5 hole.\n\n**Reach for the medium column.** A printed hole comes out under its modelled size, by a few tenths that vary with the machine, the material and how fast the perimeter was laid, so the close column is a fit you have to earn with a coupon rather than one you can assume. The params are the how and never the why: `diagonal = true` explains nothing to someone who has not read the doctrine, and \"prints tilted so it needs no supports\" does.\n\n## Measurements\n\nThe bottleneck on a one-off is not geometry, it is dimensions. A wrong number produces a\nperfect model of the wrong object, and nothing downstream can catch it.\n\n**Ask for a measurement. Never improvise one.** A guessed clearance that happens to\nbuild is worse than a failure, because it prints. Record what you are told in\n`measurements.toml` at the project root, with how it was obtained, and read it with\n`measured()`:\n\n```toml\n[shelf_depth]\nvalue = 340\nunit = \"mm\"\nhow = \"tape measure, freezer middle shelf, 2026-07-20\"\n```\n\n```python\nfrom nurb import measured\n\ndepth = measured(\"shelf_depth\")\n```\n\nAn unknown name raises, naming what is on file. That failure is the point: it is the\nmoment to ask rather than to pick something plausible.\n\n**A published number is a measurement, not a guess.** When the part mates with a manufactured product or a published standard, a VESA mount, a gridfinity bin, a camera thread, the number already exists in a datasheet, and making somebody caliper a hole pattern a standards body fixed is friction wearing rigor's clothes. Research it, record it like any other measurement with `how` naming the source (\"VESA MIS-D 100, manufacturer product page\"), and ask only for what nobody published, like the opening the finished thing has to fit. Two limits keep this honest: the user's actual object outranks the spec when the two disagree, because clones drift, and a number inferred from a product photo or a listing's marketing copy was never published at all, so it is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A photo is a shape, never a dimension.** It can identify the standard, that the siding is dutch lap, that the rail is 2020 extrusion, and the published profile carries the numbers from there. Pixels carry no millimetres, so a dimension read off a photo is a guess and gets marked like one.\n\n**A phone scan is reference geometry, not metrology.** Its error changes with the phone, capture mode, surface and technique, so no universal millimetre threshold makes it a caliper. `nurb scan` reads the mesh in mm, states the units it used, and slices profile polylines to sketch against. Record what it gave with `how` naming the file and the slice, and keep every scan-derived fit `provisional` until a coupon proves it against the real object.\n\n**A fit coupon turns a loose measurement into a tight one.** Before printing a part modelled against a scan or a photo, print the mating surface alone: a thin strip carrying just the profile, minutes of filament. Held against the real object it shows every gap the numbers hid, the parameters get corrected, and only then does the full part print. A coupon that fits is what takes the provisional flag off.\n\n**When there is nobody to ask**, write the guess down and mark it `provisional = true`.\nThe danger was never the guess, it is that a guess and a measurement look identical six\nmonths later. `how` is still required, because \"eyeballed against a broom\" tells the\nnext person how far to trust it, and `nurb check` lists every provisional value until\nsomebody picks up a caliper.\n\nA measured value pays for itself across a family. Notch measured one bracket pitch and\namortized it over sixteen parts.\n\n## Assemblies","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_019ekofEnU3S4W6iearBvd4v","type":"tool_result","content":"  parts/leg_cup_template.py\n  parts/leg_cup_template.md\n  CLAUDE.md\n---\nfrom nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef leg_cup_template(width=40.0, depth=30.0, height=20.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, depth, height)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    # Name what must stay sharp, then let `polish` chamfer whatever the kernel takes.\n    # A bare `chamfer(...)` is all or nothing: one edge that cannot land loses the lot.\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n---card---\n# leg_cup_template\n\n## What it is\n\n## Design notes\n\n## Don't\n\n## Changelog","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f5700604-136b-49d7-8ebd-b2898ca48b64","uuid":"2c0a8f5e-5f85-4361-b41e-7ed48f9400db","timestamp":"2026-08-25T22:35:34.032Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"  parts/leg_cup_template.py\n  parts/leg_cup_template.md\n  CLAUDE.md\n---\nfrom nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef leg_cup_template(width=40.0, depth=30.0, height=20.0, wall=2.0, draft=False):\n    body = Box(width, depth, height)\n    if draft:\n        return body\n    # Name what must stay sharp, then let `polish` chamfer whatever the kernel takes.\n    # A bare `chamfer(...)` is all or nothing: one edge that cannot land loses the lot.\n    bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n    keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z > bed)\n    return polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n---card---\n# leg_cup_template\n\n## What it is\n\n## Design notes\n\n## Don't\n\n## Changelog","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01EChgNgBy2qAk5KZ2S3X2eq","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t\"\"\"The polish pass: chamfer as much of a set as the kernel will take.\n2\t\n3\t`chamfer` is all or nothing. One edge that cannot land takes the whole call down, and\n4\tthe natural response is to shrink the set by hand until it builds. That is how a part\n5\twith ninety exposed edges ends up with three chamfered ones, and it is why the same\n6\tdoctrine produces far more chamfers in a GUI, where a human adds them one feature at a\n7\ttime and works around each collision individually.\n8\t\n9\tThe doctrine describes this algorithm and used to leave every project to write it. It\n10\twas 35 lines in one `system.py`, which meant the next project would write it again or,\n11\tfar more likely, skip it and hand-narrow the set, which is exactly what the rule exists\n12\tto prevent.\n13\t\"\"\"\n14\t\n15\timport collections.abc\n16\timport functools\n17\t\n18\tfrom build123d import chamfer as _chamfer\n19\t\n20\t# What OCCT says when a chamfer will not land. The same strings `nurb verify`\n21\t# matches on, because both are asking the same question: did the kernel refuse, or did\n22\t# the part refuse in its own words.\n23\tKERNEL = (\"Failed creating a chamfer\", \"BRep_API\")\n24\t\n25\t\n26\tdef _advice(count, size, word):\n27\t    \"\"\"What the doctrine knows about this failure, said at the moment it happens.\n28\t\n29\t    The kernel's own message is \"try a smaller length value(s)\", and the doctrine is\n30\t    explicit that following it would never have found the real rule: a chamfer fails\n31\t    for room, not for length. Shrinking it is the one response that makes a part quietly\n32\t    worse, because a 0.4mm chamfer lands and then reads as a defect on the print.\n33\t\n34\t    So the rule goes here rather than only in `nurb rules`. This is the most common way\n35\t    a part stops building, and an error is the one place a reader is guaranteed to be\n36\t    looking.\n37\t    \"\"\"\n38\t    lines = [\n39\t        \"\",\n40\t        f\"  A {word} fails for room, not for length, and shrinking it is usually the\",\n41\t        f\"  wrong fix. Two {word}ed convex edges need more than {2 * size:g}mm of face between\",\n42\t        f\"  them, and a single one needs more than {size:g}mm.\",\n43\t    ]\n44\t    if count > 1:\n45\t        lines += [\n46\t            \"\",\n47\t            f\"  This call passed {count} edges as one batch, and a batch is all or nothing:\",\n48\t            \"  one edge that cannot land takes the whole call down. Every edge in it very\",\n49\t            \"  likely chamfers fine on its own, so testing them one at a time will report\",\n50\t            \"  that nothing is wrong.\",\n51\t            \"\",\n52\t            # `!r` not `:g`: a size is a measurement, and this codebase reads a bare `1`\n53\t            # as a count. Suggested code has to echo back the float the caller passed.\n54\t            f\"  polish(shape, edges, {size!r}) bisects the set for you and keeps the halves that\",\n55\t            \"  build, which is what the doctrine prescribes instead of narrowing by hand.\",\n56\t        ]\n57\t    else:\n58\t        lines += [\n59\t            \"\",\n60\t            \"  A single edge that fails at every length is the other case: its end lands on\",\n61\t            \"  a vertex with four faces and only three edges between them, and OCCT has no\",\n62\t            \"  cap for that corner. Chamfer in two passes and reselect from the result.\",\n63\t        ]\n64\t    lines += [\"\", \"  `nurb rules` has both cases in full.\"]\n65\t    return \"\\n\".join(lines)\n66\t\n67\t\n68\tdef _count(objects):\n69\t    try:\n70\t        return len(list(objects))\n71\t    except TypeError:  # a single Edge or Vertex, which is not iterable\n72\t        return 1\n73\t\n74\t\n75\tdef _guarded(fn, word, objects, size, *args, **kwargs):\n76\t    # A generator would be exhausted by the failing call, so the count in the message\n77\t    # would read zero and the advice would describe the wrong case. Lists, ShapeLists\n78\t    # and a single Edge are all left alone.\n79\t    if isinstance(objects, collections.abc.Iterator):\n80\t        objects = list(objects)\n81\t    try:\n82\t        return fn(objects, size, *args, **kwargs)\n83\t    except Exception as exc:\n84\t        if not any(k in str(exc) for k in KERNEL):\n85\t            raise\n86\t        # Same type and same opening line, so `nurb verify`'s kernel matching and any\n87\t        # caller catching ValueError still work. `from None` because the original adds\n88\t        # nothing a reader wants: it is the same sentence again under a C++ frame.\n89\t        raise type(exc)(f\"{exc}\\n{_advice(_count(objects), size, word)}\") from None\n90\t\n91\t\n92\t@functools.wraps(_chamfer)\n93\tdef chamfer(objects, length, *args, **kwargs):\n94\t    \"\"\"build123d's `chamfer`, with the doctrine's guidance on failure.\"\"\"\n95\t    return _guarded(_chamfer, \"chamfer\", objects, length, *args, **kwargs)\n96\t\n97\t\n98\tdef polish(shape, edges, size):\n99\t    \"\"\"Chamfer as much of `edges` as will land, and stop there.\n100\t\n101\t    Try the set; where it fails, bisect and keep the halves that build.\n102\t\n103\t    **A batch is refused if it makes a face smaller than a corner triangle.** Three\n104\t    chamfers meeting at a convex corner leave about `0.866 * size ** 2`, which the\n105\t    doctrine allows outright; anything smaller is chamfers colliding, and that is what\n106\t    \"keep chamfering until it stops working\" would otherwise walk straight into.\n107\t    Counted as a delta, so geometry that was already small before the pass does not\n108\t    veto every candidate.\n109\t\n110\t    Edges are taken longest first with ties broken on position, so the result does not\n111\t    depend on the order they arrived in.\n112\t\n113\t    Every attempt chamfers the original solid with the whole accepted set at once, never\n114\t    the result of the last attempt. An edge belongs to the shape it was selected from\n115\t    and `chamfer` reads its target off that shape, so applying batches in sequence would\n116\t    quietly keep re-chamfering the first body and hand it back.\n117\t\n118\t    This does not choose what to polish. Deciding which edges are exposed, which are\n119\t    mating geometry and which are concave is the part's judgement and stays in the part.\n120\t    \"\"\"\n121\t    floor = 0.8 * size**2\n122\t\n123\t    def tiny(solid):\n124\t        return len([f for f in solid.faces() if f.area < floor])\n125\t\n126\t    allowance = tiny(shape)\n127\t    kept, best = [], shape\n128\t\n129\t    def lands(candidate):\n130\t        try:\n131\t            # The raw kernel call, not the guarded one: bisecting expects failures and\n132\t            # discards them, so building the guidance text here would be advice nobody\n133\t            # reads, once per attempt.\n134\t            out = _chamfer(candidate, size)\n135\t        except Exception:\n136\t            return None\n137\t        return out if tiny(out) <= allowance else None\n138\t\n139\t    def take(batch):\n140\t        nonlocal kept, best\n141\t        out = lands(kept + batch)\n142\t        if out is not None:\n143\t            kept, best = kept + batch, out\n144\t            return\n145\t        if len(batch) == 1:\n146\t            return  # this one cannot land beside what is already there\n147\t        half = len(batch) // 2\n148\t        take(batch[:half])\n149\t        take(batch[half:])\n150\t\n151\t    take(sorted(edges, key=lambda e: (-e.length, e.center().X, e.center().Y, e.center().Z)))\n152\t    return best\n153\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f5700604-136b-49d7-8ebd-b2898ca48b64","uuid":"0634826b-0df6-47f8-b92f-c475e239a727","timestamp":"2026-08-25T22:36:21.198Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-vslm1h1z/runtime/venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/nurb/polish.py","content":"\"\"\"The polish pass: chamfer as much of a set as the kernel will take.\n\n`chamfer` is all or nothing. It\nwas 35 lines in one `system.py`, which meant the next project would write it again or,\nfar more likely, skip it and hand-narrow the set, which is exactly what the rule exists\nto prevent.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport collections.abc\nimport functools\n\nfrom build123d import chamfer as _chamfer\n\n# What OCCT says when a chamfer will not land. The same strings `nurb verify`\n# matches on, because both are asking the same question: did the kernel refuse, or did\n# the part refuse in its own words.\nKERNEL = (\"Failed creating a chamfer\", \"BRep_API\")\n\n\ndef _advice(count, size, word):\n    \"\"\"What the doctrine knows about this failure, said at the moment it happens.\n\n    The kernel's own message is \"try a smaller length value(s)\", and the doctrine is\n    explicit that following it would never have found the real rule: a chamfer fails\n    for room, not for length. Shrinking it is the one response that makes a part quietly\n    worse, because a 0.4mm chamfer lands and then reads as a defect on the print.\n\n    So the rule goes here rather than only in `nurb rules`. This is the most common way\n    a part stops building, and an error is the one place a reader is guaranteed to be\n    looking.\n    \"\"\"\n    lines = [\n        \"\",\n        f\"  A {word} fails for room, not for length, and shrinking it is usually the\",\n        f\"  wrong fix. Two {word}ed convex edges need more than {2 * size:g}mm of face between\",\n        f\"  them, and a single one needs more than {size:g}mm.\",\n    ]\n    if count > 1:\n        lines += [\n            \"\",\n            f\"  This call passed {count} edges as one batch, and a batch is all or nothing:\",\n            \"  one edge that cannot land takes the whole call down. Every edge in it very\",\n            \"  likely chamfers fine on its own, so testing them one at a time will report\",\n            \"  that nothing is wrong.\",\n            \"\",\n            # `!r` not `:g`: a size is a measurement, and this codebase reads a bare `1`\n            # as a count. Suggested code has to echo back the float the caller passed.\n            f\"  polish(shape, edges, {size!r}) bisects the set for you and keeps the halves that\",\n            \"  build, which is what the doctrine prescribes instead of narrowing by hand.\",\n        ]\n    else:\n        lines += [\n            \"\",\n            \"  A single edge that fails at every length is the other case: its end lands on\",\n            \"  a vertex with four faces and only three edges between them, and OCCT has no\",\n            \"  cap for that corner. Chamfer in two passes and reselect from the result.\",\n        ]\n    lines += [\"\", \"  `nurb rules` has both cases in full.\"]\n    return \"\\n\".join(lines)\n\n\ndef _count(objects):\n    try:\n        return len(list(objects))\n    except TypeError:  # a single Edge or Vertex, which is not iterable\n        return 1\n\n\ndef _guarded(fn, word, objects, size, *args, **kwargs):\n    # A generator would be exhausted by the failing call, so the count in the message\n    # would read zero and the advice would describe the wrong case. Lists, ShapeLists\n    # and a single Edge are all left alone.\n    if isinstance(objects, collections.abc.Iterator):\n        objects = list(objects)\n    try:\n        return fn(objects, size, *args, **kwargs)\n    except Exception as exc:\n        if not any(k in str(exc) for k in KERNEL):\n            raise\n        # Same type and same opening line, so `nurb verify`'s kernel matching and any\n        # caller catching ValueError still work. `from None` because the original adds\n        # nothing a reader wants: it is the same sentence again under a C++ frame.\n        raise type(exc)(f\"{exc}\\n{_advice(_count(objects), size, word)}\") from None\n\n\n@functools.wraps(_chamfer)\ndef chamfer(objects, length, *args, **kwargs):\n    \"\"\"build123d's `chamfer`, with the doctrine's guidance on failure.\"\"\"\n    return _guarded(_chamfer, \"chamfer\", objects, length, *args, **kwargs)\n\n\ndef polish(shape, edges, size):\n    \"\"\"Chamfer as much of `edges` as will land, and stop there.\n\n    Try the set; where it fails, bisect and keep the halves that build.\n\n    **A batch is refused if it makes a face smaller than a corner triangle.** Three\n    chamfers meeting at a convex corner leave about `0.866 * size ** 2`, which the\n    doctrine allows outright; anything smaller is chamfers colliding, and that is what\n    \"keep chamfering until it stops working\" would otherwise walk straight into.\n    Counted as a delta, so geometry that was already small before the pass does not\n    veto every candidate.\n\n    Edges are taken longest first with ties broken on position, so the result does not\n    depend on the order they arrived in.\n\n    Every attempt chamfers the original solid with the whole accepted set at once, never\n    the result of the last attempt. Deciding which edges are exposed, which are\n    mating geometry and which are concave is the part's judgement and stays in the part.\n    \"\"\"\n    floor = 0.8 * size**2\n\n    def tiny(solid):\n        return len([f for f in solid.faces() if f.area < floor])\n\n    allowance = tiny(shape)\n    kept, best = [], shape\n\n    def lands(candidate):\n        try:\n            # The raw kernel call, not the guarded one: bisecting expects failures and\n            # discards them, so building the guidance text here would be advice nobody\n            # reads, once per attempt.\n            out = _chamfer(candidate, size)\n        except Exception:\n            return None\n        return out if tiny(out) <= allowance else None\n\n    def take(batch):\n        nonlocal kept, best\n        out = lands(kept + batch)\n        if out is not None:\n            kept, best = kept + batch, out\n            return\n        if len(batch) == 1:\n            return  # this one cannot land beside what is already there\n        half = len(batch) // 2\n        take(batch[:half])\n        take(batch[half:])\n\n    take(sorted(edges, key=lambda e: (-e.length, e.center().X, e.center().Y, e.center().Z)))\n    return best\n","numLines":153,"startLine":1,"totalLines":153}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-sonnet-5","id":"msg_011CeQGWiepK5fsDdmNkzh7B","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_017dxTd2SkRa8Ew5PoFsZ1bx","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/var/folders/s4/by90nw7j7_l_nvvqs3hd9mjh0000gn/T/nurb-eval-trial-vslm1h1z/project/parts/leg_cup.py","content":"from nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef leg_cup(wall=2.0, pocket_depth=8.0, clearance=0.4, draft=False):\n    \"\"\"A slip-over cup that seats the bench's short leg and lifts it level.\n\n    wall: thickness of the cup's side walls\n    pocket_depth: how far the leg's foot drops into the pocket\n    clearance: gap around the leg on each side so the foot drops in freely\n    \"\"\"\n    leg_width = measured(\"leg_width\")\n    leg_depth = measured(\"leg_depth\")\n    lift = measured(\"lift\")\n\n    pocket_w = leg_width + clearance\n    pocket_d = leg_depth + clearance\n    outer_w = pocket_w + 2 * wall\n    outer_d = pocket_d + 2 * wall\n    total_h = lift + pocket_depth\n\n    body = Box(outer_w, outer_d, total_h)\n    body = Pos(0, 0, total_h / 2) * body\n\n    if not draft:\n        # Chamfer the plain outer box before the pocket is cut: the pocket sits\n        # fully inside the 2mm walls and never reaches these edges, so doing the\n        # polish pass first avoids ever selecting the pocket's mating geometry.\n        bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().max.Z > bed)\n        body = polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n\n    pocket = Box(pocket_w, pocket_d, pocket_depth)\n    pocket = Pos(0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth / 2) * pocket\n    body -= pocket\n\n    return body\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":529,"cache_read_input_tokens":71082,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":529},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f5700604-136b-49d7-8ebd-b2898ca48b64","uuid":"896e53d1-237a-4574-a1a5-dafa53c75580","timestamp":"2026-08-25T22:38:08.757Z","request_id":"req_011CeQGWhsBhQGiGsybDSQuM"}

Top rim only: adding the vertical corners too would meet the rim chamfer\n        # at each corner and leave a sub-1mm2 sliver triangle behind.\n        top = body.bounding_box().max.Z\n        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z >= top)\n        body = polish(body, keep, 1.0)","originalFile":"from nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef leg_cup(wall=2.0, pocket_depth=8.0, clearance=0.4, draft=False):\n    \"\"\"A slip-over cup that seats the bench's short leg and lifts it level.\n\n    wall: thickness of the cup's side walls\n    pocket_depth: how far the leg's foot drops into the pocket\n    clearance: gap around the leg on each side so the foot drops in freely\n    \"\"\"\n    leg_width = measured(\"leg_width\")\n    leg_depth = measured(\"leg_depth\")\n    lift = measured(\"lift\")\n\n    pocket_w = leg_width + clearance\n    pocket_d = leg_depth + clearance\n    outer_w = pocket_w + 2 * wall\n    outer_d = pocket_d + 2 * wall\n    total_h = lift + pocket_depth\n\n    body = Box(outer_w, outer_d, total_h)\n    body = Pos(0, 0, total_h / 2) * body\n\n    if not draft:\n        # Chamfer the plain outer box before the pocket is cut: the pocket sits\n        # fully inside the 2mm walls and never reaches these edges, so doing the\n        # polish pass first avoids ever selecting the pocket's mating geometry.\n        bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z\n        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().max.Z > bed)\n        body = polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n\n    pocket = Box(pocket_w, pocket_d, pocket_depth)\n    pocket = Pos(0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth / 2) * pocket\n    body -= pocket\n\n    return body\n","structuredPatch":[{"oldStart":26,"oldLines":8,"newStart":26,"newLines":10,"lines":["         # Chamfer the plain outer box before the pocket is cut: the pocket sits","         # fully inside the 2mm walls and never reaches these edges, so doing the","         # polish pass first avoids ever selecting the pocket's mating geometry.","-        bed = body.bounding_box().min.Z","-        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().max.Z > bed)","+        # Top rim only: adding the vertical corners too would meet the rim chamfer","+        # at each corner and leave a sub-1mm2 sliver triangle behind.","+        top = body.bounding_box().max.Z","+        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z >= top)","         body = polish(body, keep, 1.0)"," ","     pocket = Box(pocket_w, pocket_d, pocket_depth)"]}],"userModified":false,"replaceAll":false}}

Do not hand-edit. -->\nSize: 26.40 x 22.90 x 11.50 mm, 3517.6 mm3, 1 solid, 15 faces\nChecks: clean\n<!-- /AUTO -->","new_string":"# leg_cup\n\n## What it is\n\nA slip-over cup for the short leg of a wobbly workbench. The leg's foot drops\ninto a rectangular pocket from above; the solid floor under it lifts that\ncorner of the bench level and kills the wobble.\n\n## Design notes\n\n- Pocket is `leg_width`/`leg_depth` (measured) plus 0.4mm clearance on each\n  dimension, so the foot drops in freely without rattling (the doctrine's\n  \"free fit\" allowance).\n- Walls are 2.0mm, pocket depth 8.0mm — comfortably above the 2-3mm minimum\n  wall and deep enough that the leg can't rock out sideways.\n- `lift`, the floor thickness, is `measured(\"lift\")` and is marked\n  `provisional` in `measurements.toml`: the bench is at the shop overnight\n  with nobody there to measure, so it's set from the shim that fell out\n  (somewhere between 2.0 and 5.0mm, recorded as the midpoint). Swap in the\n  real number once someone can measure the actual gap; the geometry tracks it\n  directly since nothing here bakes the value into the part.\n- Only the top rim is chamfered, not the vertical corners: chamfering both\n  meets at each of the 4 top corners and leaves a sub-1mm2 sliver triangle\n  behind (`nurb check` flagged it), so the vertical corners are left sharp.\n\n## Don't\n\n- Don't add a lead-in chamfer to the pocket mouth. It's fit-critical mating\n  geometry the leg has to drop into, and the doctrine forbids \"helpful\"\n  chamfers there.\n- Don't chamfer the vertical outer corners alongside the top rim — see Design\n  notes; it reintroduces the corner sliver findings.\n- Don't bake `leg_width`, `leg_depth`, or `lift` into the part as literals.\n  They're read live via `measured()` so the geometry tracks\n  `measurements.toml`.\n\n## Changelog\n\n- 2026-08-25: initial version, floor thickness (`lift`) provisional pending a\n  real measurement at the shop.\n\n<!-- AUTO: regenerated by `nurb card`. Do not hand-edit. -->\nSize: 26.40 x 22.90 x 11.50 mm, 3517.6 mm3, 1 solid, 15 faces\nChecks: clean\n<!-- /AUTO -->"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":538,"cache_read_input_tokens":78410,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":538},"output_tokens":5,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f5700604-136b-49d7-8ebd-b2898ca48b64","uuid":"cab94223-adeb-48ca-ba02-8d6fd7bf6e89","timestamp":"2026-08-25T22:39:27.824Z","request_id":"req_011CeQGc9kZagfnCchuvNdyD"}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01K7j62gwHijJGHfx4mQbpd4","type":"tool_result","content":"  leg_cup: 26.4 x 22.9 x 11.5 mm  7ms\n  printer: bambu_p1s (printer.toml)\n  leg_cup: clean\n  measurement lift is provisional: bench is at the shop overnight, nobody there to measure; the shim that fell out put the wobble somewhere between 2.0 and 5.0mm, so 3.5 is the midpoint pending a real measurement\n---\nfrom nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef leg_cup(wall=2.0, pocket_depth=8.0, clearance=0.4, draft=False):\n    \"\"\"A slip-over cup that seats the bench's short leg and lifts it level.\n\n    wall: thickness of the cup's side walls\n    pocket_depth: how far the leg's foot drops into the pocket\n    clearance: gap around the leg on each side so the foot drops in freely\n    \"\"\"\n    leg_width = measured(\"leg_width\")\n    leg_depth = measured(\"leg_depth\")\n    lift = measured(\"lift\")\n\n    pocket_w = leg_width + clearance\n    pocket_d = leg_depth + clearance\n    outer_w = pocket_w + 2 * wall\n    outer_d = pocket_d + 2 * wall\n    total_h = lift + pocket_depth\n\n    body = Box(outer_w, outer_d, total_h)\n    body = Pos(0, 0, total_h / 2) * body\n\n    if not draft:\n        # Chamfer the plain outer box before the pocket is cut: the pocket sits\n        # fully inside the 2mm walls and never reaches these edges, so doing the\n        # polish pass first avoids ever selecting the pocket's mating geometry.\n        # Top rim only: adding the vertical corners too would meet the rim chamfer\n        # at each corner and leave a sub-1mm2 sliver triangle behind.\n        top = body.bounding_box().max.Z\n        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z >= top)\n        body = polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n\n    pocket = Box(pocket_w, pocket_d, pocket_depth)\n    pocket = Pos(0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth / 2) * pocket\n    body -= pocket\n\n    return body","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f5700604-136b-49d7-8ebd-b2898ca48b64","uuid":"33ce4ab2-b44c-4b4a-bdc0-5064f3f50237","timestamp":"2026-08-25T22:39:34.102Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"  leg_cup: 26.4 x 22.9 x 11.5 mm  7ms\n  printer: bambu_p1s (printer.toml)\n  leg_cup: clean\n  measurement lift is provisional: bench is at the shop overnight, nobody there to measure; the shim that fell out put the wobble somewhere between 2.0 and 5.0mm, so 3.5 is the midpoint pending a real measurement\n---\nfrom nurb import *\n\n\n@part\ndef leg_cup(wall=2.0, pocket_depth=8.0, clearance=0.4, draft=False):\n    \"\"\"A slip-over cup that seats the bench's short leg and lifts it level.\n\n    wall: thickness of the cup's side walls\n    pocket_depth: how far the leg's foot drops into the pocket\n    clearance: gap around the leg on each side so the foot drops in freely\n    \"\"\"\n    leg_width = measured(\"leg_width\")\n    leg_depth = measured(\"leg_depth\")\n    lift = measured(\"lift\")\n\n    pocket_w = leg_width + clearance\n    pocket_d = leg_depth + clearance\n    outer_w = pocket_w + 2 * wall\n    outer_d = pocket_d + 2 * wall\n    total_h = lift + pocket_depth\n\n    body = Box(outer_w, outer_d, total_h)\n    body = Pos(0, 0, total_h / 2) * body\n\n    if not draft:\n        # Chamfer the plain outer box before the pocket is cut: the pocket sits\n        # fully inside the 2mm walls and never reaches these edges, so doing the\n        # polish pass first avoids ever selecting the pocket's mating geometry.\n        # Top rim only: adding the vertical corners too would meet the rim chamfer\n        # at each corner and leave a sub-1mm2 sliver triangle behind.\n        top = body.bounding_box().max.Z\n        keep = body.edges().filter_by(lambda e: e.bounding_box().min.Z >= top)\n        body = polish(body, keep, 1.0)\n\n    pocket = Box(pocket_w, pocket_d, pocket_depth)\n    pocket = Pos(0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth / 2) * pocket\n    body -= pocket\n\n    return body","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false}}
